[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding NumPy Strides, C-Contiguous, and Fortran-Contiguous Memory"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"To write high-performance numerical code in Python, understanding how NumPy arrays are laid out in computer memory is essential. At the core of this layout are strides and memory contiguity."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"What are NumPy Strides?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A stride defines the number of bytes to step in memory when moving from one element to the next along a specific dimension. You can inspect the strides of any NumPy array using the .strides attribute."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import numpy as np
arr = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], dtype=np.int64)
print(arr.strides)"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"For a 64-bit integer array (which takes 8 bytes per element), the strides output (24, 8) means you must jump 24 bytes to move to the next row, and 8 bytes to move to the next column."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"C-Contiguous Memory (Row-Major Order)"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"C-contiguity follows the C programming language standard, also known as row-major order. In this layout, elements of a row are stored contiguously in memory. The last dimension varies the fastest."},{"order":9,"bullet_point":"Default layout for NumPy arrays."},{"order":10,"bullet_point":"The stride of the last dimension equals the size of a single element."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"print(arr.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'])"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Fortran-Contiguous Memory (Column-Major Order)"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Fortran-contiguity follows the Fortran standard, known as column-major order. In this layout, elements of a column are stored contiguously in memory. The first dimension varies the fastest."},{"order":14,"bullet_point":"Commonly used in legacy math libraries like BLAS and LAPACK."},{"order":15,"bullet_point":"The stride of the first dimension equals the size of a single element."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"fortran_arr = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], dtype=np.int64, order='F')
print(fortran_arr.strides)
print(fortran_arr.flags['F_CONTIGUOUS'])"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Why Memory Layout Matters"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Accessing memory in a non-contiguous pattern causes cache misses, which drastically degrades performance. When writing functions that iterate over arrays, always ensure the traversal matches the underlying memory layout."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"contiguous_again = np.ascontiguousarray(fortran_arr)
print(contiguous_again.flags['C_CONTIGUOUS'])"}]
